entry.title: New in-depth issue on Skeletor, Cringer and all the He-Man heroics in ‘Masters of the Universe’
entry.summary: Issue #67 of befores & afters magazine covers the visual effects of Masters of the Universe. DIGITAL MAGAZINE members can download the issue right now from the shop post. Inspired by the original animated series that introduced He-Man and the world of Eternia to audiences in the
entry.content:
Issue #67 of befores & afters magazine covers the visual effects of Masters of the Universe.

DIGITAL MAGAZINE members can download the issue right now from the shop post.

Inspired by the original animated series that introduced He-Man and the world of Eternia to audiences in the 1980s, Travis Knight’s Masters of the Universe brings the iconic mythology into live-action for a new generation. The film, from Amazon MGM Studios, follows the story of Adam (Nicholas Galitzine), separated from his home world as a child after an attack by Skeletor (Jared Leto). Adam then returns to Eternia 15 years later after rediscovering the Sword of Power. With Skeletor now ruling the kingdom, Adam must reunite with his allies, reclaim his identity as He-Man and save his family and his world.

Realizing that world on screen required a substantial practical and digital effects effort. From the vast landscapes of Eternia and Castle Grayskull to fantastical creatures— including He-Man’s sidekick Cringer—effects artists had to translate the distinctive look and spirit of Masters of the Universe into a convincing live-action universe.

The visual effects effort was led by visual effects supervisors David Vickery and Tim Burke, with Rich Yeomans serving as visual effects producer. Chris Corbould was the film’s special effects supervisor. Prosthetics designer Barrie Gower was responsible for several practical make-up effects and prosthetics appliances on the show. VFX vendor- wise, the work was led by Industrial Light & Magic, DNEG, Rodeo FX, Cinesite, Untold Studios and Host VFX (acting as the in-house visual effects team), with previs and postvis by Proof, Inc.

In this special issue of befores & afters magazine, we speak to Vickery and a host of the main visual effects vendors about the film’s key characters, including Skeletor, He-Man, Beast Man, Cringer and Roboto. We also dive into a number of the main environments and battle sequences.

You can also grab the issue in PRINT from Amazon (that’s the US store, make sure you try your local Amazon store, too).

entry.title: Beast Man was fully CG (and the plates shot at a former RAF runway)
entry.summary: The fully CG character and the transformation of a plain backlot, in Masters of the Universe. An excerpt from issue #67 of befores & afters magazine. Beast Man (voiced by Gary Martin) in Masters of the Universe is one of Skeletor’s henchmen, and is sent to Earth to take out Adam.
entry.content:
The fully CG character and the transformation of a plain backlot, in Masters of the Universe. An excerpt from issue #67 of befores & afters magazine.

Beast Man (voiced by Gary Martin) in Masters of the Universe is one of Skeletor’s henchmen, and is sent to Earth to take out Adam. The character was completely computer-generated by ILM, and shared with other vendors. On Earth, Beast Man takes on Teela and Adam in and around a city roadway in Oklahoma City.

Proof previs’d the sequence. “We kept the Beast Man sequence simple in terms of previs, sticking to previs’ing just the shots with Beast Man and then using Travis’ animatics for the non Beast Man shots,” outlines Proof senior visualization supervisor Adam Coglan. “That was all keyframed. When we moved on to postvis we received a model and rig from ILM that we imported to Unreal. The animation was then a combination of our own keyframe stuff and ILM providing their animation files, to be rendered and comp’ed by us. The environment was a combination of the freeway section that they were building on a backlot, then extending the background to the left using reference of Oklahoma where they were shooting backplates and to the right using the section of Canary Wharf where Adam and Teela would escape. From a high perspective view, the Unreal scene looked quite oddly kitbashed together but once you were on the freeway, it made sense visually.”

During the shoot, stunt performer Clayton Grover wore a shoulder mount and an eyeline rig so that the eyeline would be correct for Beast Man. “About 20% of the shots in the final edit had some sort of physical placeholder stunt performer, but the rest of it was entirely digital,” breaks down Vickery.

The roadway was shot at Bovingdon in the UK on a former RAF runway. “They essentially took the piece of tarmac and marked it out and put up concrete bollards either side of the road, with a dozen vehicles queued up behind,” explains Vickery. “That meant the entire environment of Oklahoma City would be digital, but based on photography and scans of Oklahoma itself, as well as Canary Wharf where we shot a lot of reference of high-rise glass buildings that were appropriate.”

“I actually got a note during post-production asking me what we had done to this environment, but they hadn’t realized it was entirely digital,” laughs Vickery. “It was completely seamless. We did have the benefit of shooting it the right way. We shot it outdoors in natural daylight. The lighting was very natural.”

ILM got to building on its Beast Man asset after earlier concept art and a maquette of the character had been made. “On top of that,” shares ILM’s Ponti, “Travis supplied us with these beautiful storyboards, which were not just simple one-board-per-shot, they were almost like keyframe animation. Every shot had multiple key poses and key steps in it. From there, we also were told that the original cartoons and toys were a guiding principle. Tim Burke had also been very keen to approach this in a traditional manner, in the sense that we didn’t plan for motion capture or performance of any kind.”

Beast Man’s hair and fur, and his armor, were elements that ILM crafted after building up a reference guide. This came from the toys, at first. “We would ask questions like, for the fur around his neck, is that actual fur that’s overgrown, or is it like a piece of armor?” relates Ponti. “Some of the toys over the years have interpreted it one way or the other. We ended up going with some of the more recent toy lines where they made it like an additional piece of hide and a separate piece of armor. There was also his medallion, which we had to work out how it would dangle on him, and how all the straps worked.”

All of that design happened in tandem with motion studies, orchestrated by ILM animation supervisor Michael Lum. Ponti mentions there were discussions about leaning towards a gorilla versus a man. “In Travis’ boards, the animation was very much simian.”

For Beast Man’s face, a LiDAR scan of the maquette— which featured the character roaring—was reverse engineered by ILM into a neutral pose. “Our model supervisor, Daniel Brkovic, started doing poses for different shapes,” says Ponti. “This included roaring and being scared. They were shot-related, actions we knew he was going to do. We also had all these character sheets that we would show Travis, firstly to see if we were getting the character he wanted, but as well for us to figure out the anatomy of Beast Man’s face. At one point we also added in the face paint. This is something our lead lookdev technical director Valentina Rosselli did. She actually painted her face and took some photos and then transferred that to Beast Man.”

Ponti adds: “It was all very exciting, for another reason. ILM, of course, is famous for all our acquisition technology like Medusa and Anyma. Well, we did none of that. It was like it was the early 2000s. Beast Man was very handmade.”

That same approach was taken in terms of animation. Beast Man was predominantly achieved via keyframe animation (although Lum and his team did utilize an ILM capture stage for capturing some motion, including capture of performer James Unsworth). “What they had done on set was do a take with Clayton to get the camera moves down,” outlines Ponti. “And then they would do a clean plate, and that’s what we worked on. The performance on set was not something Travis would go back to. You don’t get that kind of freedom that often, to really go from concept, to development, to animation, when you’re making a character.”

Beast Man’s groom required several different types of fur, which were then simulated. “We have fur on his body, on his armor, called his pauldron,” details Ponti. “The fur on his head is quite matted and grimy and greasy because he’s a filthy Beast Man, of course!”

As noted, the Bovingdon airfield location was effectively a concrete backlot in place of Oklahoma City, with a range of vehicles on the set. ILM’s city build involved gathering data from Oklahoma City and Canary Wharf. “Most of the time,” says Ponti, “we would replace all the cars and all the roads, partly for reflection needs. Travis was really happy with it. We would say, ‘You will never tell that we shot this on a grubby backlot somewhere here in the UK.’ In truth, it was quite challenging because it was a very changing season when the shoot happened. There were days when it was pouring down and days where it was really sunny. As a result, we had to do a ton of work to just make it all fit together, and to justify the sun in the background.”

New in-depth issue on Skeletor, Cringer and all the He-Man heroics in ‘Masters of the Universe’

“That was something I loved about working with David Vickery on this,” continues Ponti. “David knew we were doing a good job with the environment itself, and his main focus was about the continuity. He’d say, ‘Maybe we could put a bit of sun coming through there, or add a bit of shadow from a pretend building off-screen here.’ It really helped make it seamless.”

Having escaped Beast Man on Earth, Teela and Adam return to Eternia in Teela’s ship by ‘bending space’. They embark on a hyperspace-tunnel-like journey through a rainbow-colored rift back to their home planet. ILM created this effect, having also generated a similar look for young Adam journeying to Earth years earlier.

“Travis had a very clear idea of what this should be, although it was also a very abstract thing,” advises Ponti. “There was a desire of it being as grounded as possible, while also being very organic. As we developed the transformation and other effects in the movie that were working really well, we started integrating some of those elements back into the rift. This idea of echoes—outlines of the objects inside the rift, such as the spaceship, or Adam, they actually worked really well, so there was this 80s taste to it. And then of course, the saturation, the colorfulness, that’s one of the biggest notes that Travis would give us.”

Some of the earliest looks for the rift were based on slit- scan techniques, inspired by the Star Gate sequence in 2001: A Space Odyssey and the original Doctor Who opening. “That’s why initially we leant heavily into the environment out of the trails of the people inside the environment,” says Ponti. “In the end, we settled on something a little different because we needed the audience to understand what they were looking at. Still, we managed to input a bit more depth in there with some of these trails.”

entry.title: Reallusion and Escape.AI Partner to Solve AI Video Bottlenecks and Expand Distribution
entry.summary: Strategic alliance connects Reallusion’s 3D ecosystem with John Gaeta’s Neo Cinema platform, bringing consistent AI filmmaking to 400 million Connected TVs. Reallusion Inc. , the leader in 3D character generation and real-time animation software, and Escape.AI Media Inc. , the pr
entry.content:
Strategic alliance connects Reallusion’s 3D ecosystem with John Gaeta’s Neo Cinema platform, bringing consistent AI filmmaking to 400 million Connected TVs.

Reallusion Inc., the leader in 3D character generation and real-time animation software, and Escape.AI Media Inc., the premier “Neo Cinema” content platform and creator marketplace, today announced a strategic partnership. The multi-year alliance addresses critical generative AI video challenges, including visual inconsistencies, high token costs, and ambiguous IP ownership. Together, the companies establish a robust 3D-to-AI pipeline for professional AI storytellers.

Creators using generative AI video frequently encounter shifting character designs and high render costs, while text-generated content faces legal scrutiny regarding copyright eligibility. Reallusion and Escape.AI solve these challenges by using 3D spatial data as a precise control layer. Grounding generative models in human-authored assets ensures frame-to-frame continuity and undeniable proof of original authorship.

Reallusion’s Full-Circle 3D Ecosystem: The Structural Engine for AI

Under the agreement, Reallusion integrates its full-circle 3D software and asset infrastructure with a 3D-to-AI Video Workflow into the Escape.AI creator ecosystem:

  • Character Creator 5 (CC5): Enables creators to design custom, fully rigged 3D characters with precise facial blendshapes and high-resolution textures. These base 3D files serve as the original IP foundation that can be trained into custom AI models with absolute visual continuity.
  • ActorCore Motion Library: Provides thousands of professionally captured, high-quality 3D motion animations, rigged characters, props, and facial expressions optimized for film, gaming, and simulation workflows.
  • iClone Real-Time Animation Software: Offers real-time scene setup, motion clip editing, motion blending, camera path control, and lighting direction. This 3D environment acts as an exact physical blueprint to guide generative video models, drastically reducing AI hallucinations.
  • Reallusion AI Studio: A standalone creation app that ingests 3D scene data from iClone and CC5 as a precision control layer. By integrating leading generative AI models with highly optimized backend prompts, AI Studio ensures frame-by-frame temporal consistency while dramatically cutting cloud rendering token costs.

“Pure text-to-video generation has hit a hard ceiling when it comes to long-form narrative storytelling,” said Enoc Burgos, Director of Reallusion Inc. “Filmmakers cannot build persistent franchises when characters and animations morph from shot to shot. By pairing Reallusion’s 3D control layer with AI Studio, we give directors total camera, spatial, lighting, and motion command over their scenes. More importantly, our alliance with Escape empowers creators by placing powerful 3D tools directly alongside a premier path to global distribution and monetization, ensuring artists retain verifiable IP ownership over their original characters and worlds.”

Escape.AI: Global CTV Distribution and Monetization

Complementing Reallusion’s creation engine, Escape.AI provides a curated, prestige distribution layer for independent AI filmmakers. Founded by Academy Award-winning visual effects pioneer John Gaeta, Escape.AI operates a “Neo Cinema” streaming ecosystem designed to bypass algorithm-driven social feeds in favor of gallery-quality presentation.

Key benefits of the Escape.AI platform include:

  • Global Connected TV (CTV) Footprint: Through core distribution partnerships with networks like Play.Works, Escape.AI broadcasts curated short-form films, episodic series, and visual music directly to living rooms on Roku, Amazon Fire TV, LG Smart TVs, and Samsung Smart TVs, accessing an addressable market exceeding 400 million active CTV devices.
  • Prestige Curation: Modeled after flagship visual anthologies such as Love, Death & Robots, Escape.AI elevates high-craft AI cinema across specialized genres including Sci-Fi, Fantasy, Horror, and Anime.
  • Transparent Creator Monetization: Creators distributing on Escape.AI participate in a 50% net revenue split for syndicated Connected TV content, direct audience patronage and tipping, custom channel subscriptions, and digital collectibles—all while retaining 100% ownership of their underlying intellectual property.

“Neo Cinema is about blending human imagination, game engine control, and generative AI into a unified narrative force,” said John Gaeta, Founder of Escape.AI Media Inc. “Reallusion provides the precise 3D skeleton and camera guidance that generative models desperately need to achieve cinematic discipline. By combining Reallusion’s powerful toolset with Escape’s distribution network, this partnership empowers and expands a growing community of talented filmmakers, giving them the control to craft world-class, consistent stories and the global showcase to broadcast them to hundreds of millions of screens worldwide.”

Joint Initiatives & Community Access: Escape Labs

To empower the next generation of AI filmmakers, Reallusion and Escape.AI are launching:

  1. Escape Labs Portal: Features workflow guides, asset packs, and reference blueprints showcasing CC5, iClone, and AI Studio at escape.ai/labs/tools.
  2. Community Access: Offers free access to iClone PERSONAL for the Escape.AI creator community to build 3D control layers.
  3. Masterclasses & Demos: Co-hosted workshops and a flagship joint Live Demo event on October 23, 2026, demonstrating real-time 3D-to-AI workflows.
  4. Creator Grants: Direct 3D and AI technical support, along with AI point sponsorships, for select directors participating in an elite program of creators.

About Reallusion Inc.

Reallusion Inc. (reallusion.com) is a leader in 3D character animation and software development that specializes in 3D character generation and real-time animation software. Its flagship tools including Character Creator, iClone, ActorCore, and AI Studio—empower filmmakers, game studios, and VFX artists worldwide to accelerate production and bridge 3D graphics with generative AI Creation workflows.

Website: https://www.reallusion.com
AI Studio: https://ai.reallusion.com/ai-studio/

About Escape.AI Media Inc.

Founded by Academy Award-winner John Gaeta (The Matrix), Escape.AI (escape.ai) is a next-generation “Neo Cinema” distribution platform and creator marketplace for AI-driven short films, experimental storytelling, and visual arts. Backed by an advisory board of veterans from Pixar, Lucasfilm, Epic Games, Disney, and Google, Escape.AI brings curated, high-craft AI cinema out of crowded social feeds and into living rooms worldwide via native Connected TV (CTV) applications reaching over 400 million active devices.

Website: https://escape.ai
